    Association,

              Plaintiff,

14                                                                        
15        Pending before the Court is Defendant Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.'s ("Wells Fargo") 
16   Motion to Dismiss Count One pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) (Doc. 
17   6) and Defendant Washington Federal Bank's ("WaFd") Motion to Dismiss Count One 
18   pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) (Doc. 16). The matters have been 
19   fully briefed. (Docs. 6, 13, 16, 21, 23–24.) Per the parties' request, the Court held oral 
20   argument on April 16, 2024.                                          
21     I.   Factual Allegations                                           
22        This case was removed from state court based on diversity jurisdiction. (Doc. 1.) 
23   Plaintiff Green Valley Villas West Condominium Association ("Villas West") filed suit 
24   against WaFd and Wells Fargo. (Doc. 1-3 at 5–9.) In 2020, Villas West hired Jesus 
25   Sotelo  to  do  administrative  work;  unbeknownst  to  Villas  West,  Sotelo  devised  two 
26   schemes to embezzle money from his employer. (Id. at 5–6.)           
27        In the first scheme, Sotelo took invoices from vendors who did work for Villas 
28   West and forged new invoices for inflated amounts that he submitted to Villas West for 
1   payment. (Id.) Villas West had two bank accounts with WaFd. (Id.) Once Villas West 
2   issued checks from one of these accounts to pay the inflated invoices, Sotelo deposited 
3   the checks into one of his personal bank accounts at Wells Fargo via ATM or the Wells 
4   Fargo mobile banking app. (Id.) Sotelo then sent payment directly from his account to the 
5   vendor for the originally invoiced amount. (Id.)                     
6        According to the Complaint, Sotelo deposited at least 53 inflated vendor checks 
7   from  October  1,  2020  to  September  8,  2021.  (Id.)  Most  of  those  checks  had  no 
8   indorsement signature; on the others, Sotelo simply wrote the name of the vendor to 
9   indorse the check. (Id.) Sotelo allegedly stole $234,570.60 by depositing inflated vendor 
10   checks. (Id.)                                                        
11        In his second scheme, Sotelo deposited checks mailed and issued to Villas West 
12   into his personal accounts at Wells Fargo. (Id.) Sotelo again deposited the un-indorsed 
13   checks  via  ATM  or  mobile  banking  app.  (Id.)  Villas  West  alleges  that  Sotelo  stole 
14   $86,965.38 by depositing checks issued to Villas West. (Id.)         
         Villas West alleges that neither WaFd nor Wells Fargo exercised ordinary care or 
15                                                                        
    followed  internal  policies  for  validating  check  indorsements,  in  particular  for  large 
16                                                                        
    checks. (Id. at 6–7.) For example, Sotelo deposited an inflated vendor check for $31,000 
17                                                                        
    and a check issued to Villas West for $68,758.38. (Id.)              
18                                                                        
         Count One—based on the vendor check scheme—is titled "Recredit Account" and 
19                                                                        
    alleges that both WaFd and Wells Fargo "failed to act in a commercially reasonable 
20                                                                        
    manner when they allowed Sotelo to deposit vendor checks into his account that were 
21                                                                        
    neither made out to him nor properly indorsed." (Id. at 7.) As a result, Plaintiffs allege 
22                                                                        
    WaFd and Wells Fargo "must recredit Plaintiffs' [sic] accounts . . . ." (Id.) Count Two—
23                                                                        
    based on the second embezzlement scheme—is titled as a Uniform Commercial Code 
24                                                                        
    ("UCC") Conversion claim and alleges that Wells Fargo "failed to act in a commercially 
25                                                                        
    reasonable manner when it allowed Sotelo to deposit checks into his account that were 
26                                                                        
    clearly payable to Plaintiff and that were not properly indorsed." (Id. at 8.) Only Count 
27                                                                        
    One is at issue on the pending Motions to Dismiss.                   
28                                                                        
1     II.  Motion to Dismiss Standard                                    
2        Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) "tests the legal sufficiency of a claim" 
3   and  allows  a  party  to  seek  dismissal  for  failure  to  state  a  claim  because  either  the 
4   complaint lacks a cognizable legal theory or lacks the factual allegations to support such 
5   a theory. Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001); see also Balistreri v. 
6   Pacifica Police Dep't, 901 F.2d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1990). "[A] complaint must contain 
7   sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to 'state a claim to relief that is plausible on its 
8   face.'" Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 
9   550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)).                                           
10        A claim is only plausible "when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the 
11   court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct 
12   alleged." Id. The law requires the complaint to contain more than "a statement of facts 
13   that merely creates a suspicion [of] a legally cognizable right of action." Twombly, 550 
14   U.S. at 555. This means that "[t]hreadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, 
    supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice." Id.        
15                                                                        
         "As a general rule, a district court may not consider any material beyond the 
16                                                                        
    pleadings in ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion." Lee v. City of L.A., 250 F.3d 668, 688 
17                                                                        
    (9th Cir. 2001). A court may, however, consider documents not attached to the complaint 
18                                                                        
    without converting the motion to one for summary judgment if the "'authenticity . . . is 
19                                                                        
    not contested' and 'the plaintiff's complaint necessarily relies' on them."  Id. (quoting 
20                                                                        
    Parrino v. FHP, Inc., 146 F.3d 699, 705–06 (9th Cir. 1998)).         
21                                                                        
      III.  Wells Fargo's Motion to Dismiss                              
22                                                                        
         Wells  Fargo  seeks  to  dismiss  Count  One  pursuant  to  Federal  Rule  of  Civil 
23                                                                        
    Procedure 12(b)(6). (Doc. 6 at 1.) The Complaint does not specify what statute underpins 
24                                                                        
    Count  One.  (See  Doc.  1.)  Wells  Fargo  assumes  that,  because  Count  One  seeks  to 
25                                                                        
    "recredit" an account, it is governed by UCC §§ 3-420 and 4-401 (A.R.S. §§ 47-3420 and 
26                                                                        
    47-4401)1 and it argues that, under both provisions, the claim fails as a matter of law. 
27                                                                        

28             1 The parties use citations to the UCC, but this Order will cite 
              the  equivalent  provisions  in  the  Arizona  Revised  Statutes 
1   (Doc. 6 at 2.) First, Wells Fargo asserts that § 47-3420 "fails because the issuer of a 
2   check may not bring an action for its conversion" and Villas West issued the vendor 
3   checks alleged in Count One. (Id. at 6.) Second, Wells Fargo argues that § 47-4401 
4   cannot support a plausible claim because "[o]nly the customer's own bank—i.e., the 
5   drawee or payor bank—may 'charge' its customer's account [and] [t]hus, the customer 
6   may only bring a claim to recredit account (to reverse the charge) against its own bank." 
7   (Id. at 7.) Because Wells Fargo was Sotelo's bank, Villas West can only bring a recredit 
8   account action against WaFd. (Id. at  7–8.)                          
9        However, in its Response, Villas West emphasizes that the Complaint cannot be 
10   dismissed simply because it failed to specify a particular legal theory. (Doc. 13 at 4.) 
11   Rather, Villas West seeks "reimbursement under any applicable legal theory of the funds 
12   that it lost because of Wells Fargo's failure to employ commercially-reasonable banking 
13   practices." (Id.) More specifically, Villas West clarifies that Count One is governed by 
14   A.R.S. §§ 47-3404 to 47-3406 and both these provisions hold a depository bank liable. 
    (Id. at 1.)                                                          
15                                                                        
         Addressing these statutes for the first time in its Reply, Wells Fargo argues that § 
16                                                                        
    47-3404 applies only in situations where there was an "imposter" or "fictitious payee" 
17                                                                        
    and neither is involved here. (Doc. 21 at 2.) It emphasizes that Villas West made the 
18                                                                        
    checks out to the correct vendors, and Sotelo was not impersonating the vendor nor 
19                                                                        
    inducing Villas West to write the check in his name. (Id.) Moreover, Wells Fargo asserts 
20                                                                        
    that any § 47-3404 claim would fail as to any checks that were not indorsed because that 
21                                                                        
    provision only applies to indorsed checks. (Id. at 3 n.2.)           
22                                                                        
         Similarly, Wells Fargo argues that a claim under § 47-3405 fails because Villas 
23                                                                        
    West has not plausibly alleged that Wells Fargo failed to exercise ordinary care. (Id. at 4.) 
24                                                                        
    Specifically, "Plaintiff does not allege that Wells Fargo had a prescribed procedure to 
25                                                                        
    examine any of the checks at issue . . . ." (Id.) Wells Fargo avers that it does not have any 
26                                                                        
    such procedure, especially for checks as little as $31,000 and, even if it did, those checks 
27                                                                        

28             because that is the applicable authority. Arizona adopted the 
              UCC. See Title 47, Arizona Revised Statutes.               
1   were not indorsed and the statute only applies to indorsed checks. (Id. at 5.) Furthermore, 
2   Wells Fargo highlights that § 47-3103(A)(7) does not require a bank to examine checks 
3   deposited via automated means in order to exercise ordinary care. (Id.)  
4        The remainder of the Reply focuses on Wells Fargo's argument that § 47-3406 
5   does not provide an affirmative claim but is rather a contributory negligence provision 
6   applicable only where a defendant asserts that the issuer of a check also failed to exercise 
7   ordinary care. (Id. at 6–9.)                                         
8             A. Discussion                                              
9        As a threshold matter, Villas West is correct that Count One cannot be dismissed 
10   because the Complaint failed to specify a legal theory. "A complaint does not need to 
11   specify the particular legal theory on which a claim is based 'so long as sufficient factual 
12   averments show that the claimant may be entitled to some relief.'" Robinson v. Managed 
13   Accounts Receivables Corp., 654 F. Supp. 2d 1051, 1058 (C.D. Cal. 2009) (quoting 
14   Fontana v. Haskin, 262 F.3d 871, 877 (9th Cir. 2001)); see also Braiser v. Union Pac. 
    R.R., No. CV-21-00065-TUC-JGZ (MSA), 2023 WL 2754007, at *14 (D. Ariz. Mar. 31, 
15                                                                        
    2023).                                                               
16                                                                        
         The Court also notes that Villas West does not clearly assert a stand-alone cause of 
17                                                                        
    action based on § 47-3406. Instead, it raises the provision in the context of explaining 
18                                                                        
    that §§ 47-3404, 47-3405, and 47-3406 create a negligence cause of action framework 
19                                                                        
    against depository banks and other courts have concluded as much when applying these 
20                                                                        
    provisions to embezzlement schemes similar to the ones at issue in this case. (Doc. 13 at 
21                                                                        
    5–6.) Indeed, Villas West agreed at oral argument with Wells Fargo that § 47-3406 
22                                                                        
    permits a bank to assert that the issuer of a check was contributorily negligent. The Court 
23                                                                        
    therefore finds it unnecessary to examine whether § 47-3406 is an offensive tool that 
24                                                                        
    provides a stand-alone cause of action because Villas West is not seeking to use it as 
25                                                                        
    such. Therefore, in this Order, the Court will only  discuss whether Count One may 
26                                                                        
    proceed under §§ 47-3404 and 47-3405.                                
27                                                                        
         First, the Court finds that Villas West has plead a claim against Wells Fargo in 
28                                                                        
    Count One under § 47-3404. Assuming the facts alleged are true, Sotelo's vendor check 
1   scheme was plausibly an imposter situation. An imposter situation occurs where "an 
2   imposter . . . induces the issuer of [the] instrument to issue the instrument to the imposter 
3   . . . by impersonating the payee of the instrument . . . ." A.R.S. § 47-3404(A). Subsection 
4   D establishes liability when an imposter deposits a check:           
5             [I]f a person paying the [imposter] instrument or taking it for 
              value or for collection fails to exercise ordinary care in paying 
6                                                                        
              or  taking  the  instrument  and  that  failure  substantially 
7             contributes to loss resulting from payment of the instrument, 
              the  person  bearing  the  loss  may  recover  from  the  person 
8                                                                        
              failing to exercise ordinary care to the extent the failure to 
9             exercise ordinary care contributed to the loss.            

10        A.R.S. § 47-3404(D) (emphasis added).                           
11        Ordinary care is the "observance of reasonable commercial standards, prevailing in 
12   the area in which the person is located, with respect to the business in which the person is 
13   engaged." A.R.S. § 47-3103(A)(7). "In the case of a bank that takes an instrument for 
14   processing  for  collection  or  payment  by  automated  means,  reasonable  commercial 
15   standards do not require the bank to examine the instrument if the failure to examine does 
16   not  violate  the  bank's  prescribed  procedures  and  the  bank's  procedures  do  not  vary 
17   unreasonably from general banking usage not disapproved by this chapter or chapter 4 of 
18   this title." Id. (emphasis added). However, the comments make clear that the customer is 
19   not precluded "from proving that the procedures followed by a bank are unreasonable, 
20   arbitrary, or unfair." A.R.S. § 47-3103 cmt. 4.                      
21        Although Villas West does not allege that Sotelo induced it to issue vendor checks 
22   in his name, Villas West does allege that Sotelo induced it to write inflated vendor checks 
23   with the sole purpose of depositing the money into his account thereby impersonating the 
24   payee. Furthermore, Villas West specifically alleges that Wells Fargo failed to exercise 
25   ordinary  care  because  it  "failed  to  follow  any  internal  policies  for  validating  check 
26   endorsements . . . ." (Doc. 1-3 at 7.)                               
27        The issues Wells Fargo raised in its briefings and at oral argument are factual 
    questions suitable for summary judgment but not a motion to dismiss. These include 
28                                                                        
1   whether Wells Fargo has any policy of verifying checks deposited through automated 
2   means; whether that policy requires Wells Fargo to confirm that the checks are indorsed 
3   and payable to the account holder; whether Wells Fargo's actions in permitting Sotelo to 
4   deposit 53 checks made out to other payees violated any such policy; or whether Wells 
5   Fargo's procedures are otherwise unreasonable, arbitrary, or unfair.  
6         The Court likewise finds that Villas West has plausibly alleged a claim in Count 
7   One based on § 47-3405. That provision covers situations where an employee "entrusted 
8   with responsibility with respect to the instrument . . . makes a fraudulent indorsement of 
9   the instrument," establishing that such indorsement "is effective as the indorsement of the 
10   person to whom the instrument is payable if it is made in the name of that person." A.R.S. 
11   § 47-3405(B). Despite the employer's own liability, the employer may also recover from 
12   "the person paying the instrument or taking it for value or for collection [if the person] 
13   fails  to  exercise  ordinary  care  in  paying  or  taking  the  instrument  and  that  failure 
14   substantially contributes to loss resulting from the fraud." Id.     
         Again, for purposes of a motion to dismiss, Villas West's allegations establish that 
15                                                                        
    it  hired  Sotelo  as  an  employee  and  entrusted  him  with  responsibility  regarding  the 
16                                                                        
    invoices and the checks made payable to vendors. It also alleged that on some of those 
17                                                                        
    checks, Sotelo made fraudulent indorsements by writing the name of the vendor, and, on 
18                                                                        
    the rest, he simply fraudulently indorsed them by depositing the checks into his personal 
19                                                                        
    accounts.                                                            
20                                                                        
         The same factual questions that arise with regard to § 47-3404 arise with § 47-
21                                                                        
    3405 and can be raised at summary judgment. Moreover, the issue of whether these 
22                                                                        
    statutes can apply to checks that were not indorsed through signature was presented for 
23                                                                        
    the first time in Wells Fargo's Reply and has not been fully briefed. The Court will not 
24                                                                        
    determine at this stage whether Wells Fargo or WaFd are entitled to a judgment in their 
25                                                                        
    favor as to the un-indorsed checks.                                  
26                                                                        
         Because Villas West has plead a plausible claim in Count One, the Court will deny 
27                                                                        
    Wells Fargo's Motion to Dismiss.                                     
28                                                                        
    ///                                                                  
1     IV.  WaFd's Motion to Dismiss                                      
2        WaFd seeks to dismiss Count One pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) because it argues that 
3   Villa West's claims are time-barred by both the Business Deposit Account Agreement 
4   between Villas West and WaFd ("the Agreement") and the UCC. (Doc. 16 at 1.)  
5        The Agreement between WaFd and Villas West requires Villas West to notify 
6   WaFd about unauthorized transactions within 30 days after the account statement is made 
7   available. (Id.) By signing the Agreement, WaFd argues, "Villas West agreed not to 
8   assert any claim against WaFd Bank for unauthorized transactions not reported within 
9   this time frame." (Id.) Furthermore, the Agreement precludes actions based on repeated 
10   unauthorized transactions by a single individual if the first unauthorized transaction is not 
11   reported. (Id.) Because Villas West did not notify WaFd until two years after the checks 
12   were deposited, WaFd argues this claim should be dismissed. (Id.)    
13        WaFd also argues that A.R.S. § 47-4406(F) requires that "a customer like Villas 
14   West suing its own bank on a claim stemming from a non-indorsed (or fraudulently 
    indorsed) check(s) drawn against its account must 'discover and report' any such concerns 
15                                                                        
    to the bank within one year after the monthly account statement becomes available to the 
16                                                                        
    customer . . . ." (Id. at 1–2.) Villas West's claims therefore fail, according to WaFd, 
17                                                                        
    because this lawsuit was not filed until nearly two years after the embezzlement began. 
18                                                                        
    (Id. at 2.)                                                          
19                                                                        
         Villas  West  responds  that,  to  the  extent  the  Court  is  willing  to  consider  the 
20                                                                        
    Agreement at this stage, it does not preclude Count One because Villas West could not 
21                                                                        
    have discovered the fraud by looking at the account statements. (Doc. 23 at 5.) Further, it 
22                                                                        
    argues that § 47-4406(F) is inapplicable because the statute only applies to checks with 
23                                                                        
    an unauthorized signature or alteration. (Id. at 4.) Villas West also cites to Comment 5 of 
24                                                                        
    the UCC § 4-406 (the provision that A.R.S. § 47-4406 adopted) which states that the 
25                                                                        
    UCC does not impose a duty on the customer to timely discover fraud based on a forged 
26                                                                        
    indorsement. (Id.)                                                   
27                                                                        
    ///                                                                  
28                                                                        
    ///                                                                  
1          A. Discussion                                                 
2        As a threshold matter, the Court will not consider the Agreement at this stage. "As 
3   a general rule, a district court may not consider any material beyond the pleadings in 
4   ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion." Lee v. City of L.A., 250 F.3d 668, 688 (9th Cir. 2001). 
5   A  court  may,  however,  consider  documents  not  attached  to  the  complaint  without 
6   converting the motion to one for summary judgment if the "'authenticity . . . is not 
7   contested' and 'the plaintiff's complaint necessarily relies' on them." Id. (quoting Parrino 
8   v. FHP, Inc., 146 F.3d 699, 705–06 (9th Cir. 1998)).                 
9        The Agreement here is material beyond the pleadings and Villas West's Complaint 
10   does not necessarily rely on its account contract with WaFd. Neither did WaFd address 
11   how it argues that the Court should consider this document. Because the Court has not 
12   converted WaFd's Motion to Dismiss, the Agreement is not determinative at this stage. 
13   The factual questions regarding the meaning of the terms of the Agreement and whether 
14   Villas West's claims were discoverable within the meaning of these terms may be raised 
    at summary judgment.                                                 
15                                                                        
         The Court also finds that Villas West's claim against WaFd is timely under the 
16                                                                        
    UCC (A.R.S. Title 47). WaFd relies on the one-year statute of limitations in § 47-4406(F) 
17                                                                        
    for claims brought by a customer against its bank based on unauthorized signatures or 
18                                                                        
    alterations to transactions. Section 47-4406(F) reads:               
19                                                                        
              Without regard to care or lack of care of either the customer 
20                                                                        
              or the bank, a customer who does not within one year after 
21             the statement or items are made available to the customer . . . 
              discover and report the customer's unauthorized signature on 
22                                                                        
              or  any  alteration  on  the  item  is  precluded  from  asserting 
23             against the bank the unauthorized signature or alteration. 

24   A.R.S. § 47-4406(F) (emphasis added). However, Comment 5 specifically excludes any 
25   responsibility for an account holder to discover forged indorsements. A.R.S. § 47-4406 
26   cmt.  5  ("Section  4-406  imposes  no  duties  on  the  drawer  to  look  for  unauthorized 
27   indorsements."). The majority of the checks here were not indorsed and did not contain 
28   any alteration or unauthorized signature. Therefore, §47-4406(F)'s one-year statute of 
   ||  limitations does not apply. 
2          Rather, it is the three-year statute of limitations set out in § 47-4111 for all claims 
3||    brought under Title 47 that governs. The first of the vendor checks was issued on October 
       1,  2020  (paid  October  5,  2020)  and  the  last  was  issued  September  8,  2021  (paid 
5||    September 9,  2021).  (Doc.  1,  Ex.  A.  at 4,  56.) Villas West filed  suit on July  6,  2023. 
6||    (Doc.  1.)  Because  Villas  West  commenced  this  action  within  three  years  of  Sotelo 
      depositing the vendor checks, the claim is timely and the Court will deny WaFd's Motion 
8 ||  to Dismiss. 
9       V.     Conclusion 
10          For the foregoing reasons, 
11          IT IS ORDERED that Defendant Wells Fargo's Motion to Dismiss is DENIED. 
      (Doc. 6.) 
13          IT  IS  FURTHER  ORDERED  that  Defendant  WaFd's  Motion  to  Dismiss  is 
  ||  DENIED. (Doc. 16.) 
15          Dated this 18th day of April, 2024.

3   and  allows  a  party  to  seek  dismissal  for  failure  to  state  a  claim  because  either  the

5   a theory. Navarro v. Block,
250 F.3d 729, 732
 (9th Cir. 2001); see also Balistreri v. 
6   Pacifica Police Dep't,
901 F.2d 696, 699
 (9th Cir. 1990). "[A] complaint must contain 
7   sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to 'state a claim to relief that is plausible on its 
8   face.'" Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 
9
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007)).                                           
10        A claim is only plausible "when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the 
11   court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct 
12   alleged."
Id.
 The law requires the complaint to contain more than "a statement of facts 
13   that merely creates a suspicion [of] a legally cognizable right of action." Twombly, 550 
14   U.S. at 555. This means that "[t]hreadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, 
    supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice." Id.        
15                                                                        
         "As a general rule, a district court may not consider any material beyond the 
16                                                                        
    pleadings in ruling on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion." Lee v. City of L.A.,
250 F.3d 668
, 688 
17                                                                        
    (9th Cir. 2001). A court may, however, consider documents not attached to the complaint 
18                                                                        
    without converting the motion to one for summary judgment if the "'authenticity . . . is 
19                                                                        
    not contested' and 'the plaintiff's complaint necessarily relies' on them."
Id.
 (quoting 
20                                                                        
    Parrino v. FHP, Inc.,
146 F.3d 699
, 705–06 (9th Cir. 1998)).

8             A. Discussion                                              
9        As a threshold matter, Villas West is correct that Count One cannot be dismissed 
10   because the Complaint failed to specify a legal theory. "A complaint does not need to 
11   specify the particular legal theory on which a claim is based 'so long as sufficient factual 
12   averments show that the claimant may be entitled to some relief.'" Robinson v. Managed 
13   Accounts Receivables Corp.,
654 F. Supp. 2d 1051, 1058
 (C.D. Cal. 2009) (quoting 
14   Fontana v. Haskin,
262 F.3d 871, 877
 (9th Cir. 2001)); see also Braiser v. Union Pac.

2023 WL 2754007
, at *14 (D. Ariz. Mar. 31, 
15

16

17

18                                                                        
    that §§ 47-3404, 47-3405, and 47-3406 create a negligence cause of action framework 
19                                                                        
    against depository banks and other courts have concluded as much when applying these 
20                                                                        
    provisions to embezzlement schemes similar to the ones at issue in this case. (Doc. 13 at 
21                                                                        
    5–6.) Indeed, Villas West agreed at oral argument with Wells Fargo that § 47-3406 
22

23

24

25

26

27                                                                        
         First, the Court finds that Villas West has plead a claim against Wells Fargo in 
28                                                                        
    Count One under § 47-3404. Assuming the facts alleged are true, Sotelo's vendor check 
1   scheme was plausibly an imposter situation. An imposter situation occurs where "an 
2   imposter . . . induces the issuer of [the] instrument to issue the instrument to the imposter 
3   . . . by impersonating the payee of the instrument . . . ." A.R.S. § 47-3404(A). Subsection 
4   D establishes liability when an imposter deposits a check:           
5             [I]f a person paying the [imposter] instrument or taking it for 
              value or for collection fails to exercise ordinary care in paying 
6                                                                        
              or  taking  the  instrument  and  that  failure  substantially 
7             contributes to loss resulting from payment of the instrument, 
              the  person  bearing  the  loss  may  recover  from  the  person 
8                                                                        
              failing to exercise ordinary care to the extent the failure to 
9             exercise ordinary care contributed to the loss.            

10        A.R.S. § 47-3404(D) (emphasis added).                           
11        Ordinary care is the "observance of reasonable commercial standards, prevailing in 
12   the area in which the person is located, with respect to the business in which the person is 
13   engaged." A.R.S. § 47-3103(A)(7). "In the case of a bank that takes an instrument for 
14   processing  for  collection  or  payment  by  automated  means,  reasonable  commercial 
15   standards do not require the bank to examine the instrument if the failure to examine does 
16   not  violate  the  bank's  prescribed  procedures  and  the  bank's  procedures  do  not  vary 
17   unreasonably from general banking usage not disapproved by this chapter or chapter 4 of 
18   this title." Id. (emphasis added). However, the comments make clear that the customer is 
19   not precluded "from proving that the procedures followed by a bank are unreasonable, 
20   arbitrary, or unfair." A.R.S. § 47-3103 cmt. 4.                      
21        Although Villas West does not allege that Sotelo induced it to issue vendor checks 
22   in his name, Villas West does allege that Sotelo induced it to write inflated vendor checks 
23   with the sole purpose of depositing the money into his account thereby impersonating the 
24   payee. Furthermore, Villas West specifically alleges that Wells Fargo failed to exercise 
25   ordinary  care  because  it  "failed  to  follow  any  internal  policies  for  validating  check 
26   endorsements . . . ." (Doc. 1-3 at 7.)                               
27        The issues Wells Fargo raised in its briefings and at oral argument are factual 
    questions suitable for summary judgment but not a motion to dismiss. These include 
28                                                                        
1   whether Wells Fargo has any policy of verifying checks deposited through automated 
2   means; whether that policy requires Wells Fargo to confirm that the checks are indorsed 
3   and payable to the account holder; whether Wells Fargo's actions in permitting Sotelo to 
4   deposit 53 checks made out to other payees violated any such policy; or whether Wells 
5   Fargo's procedures are otherwise unreasonable, arbitrary, or unfair.  
6         The Court likewise finds that Villas West has plausibly alleged a claim in Count 
7   One based on § 47-3405. That provision covers situations where an employee "entrusted 
8   with responsibility with respect to the instrument . . . makes a fraudulent indorsement of 
9   the instrument," establishing that such indorsement "is effective as the indorsement of the 
10   person to whom the instrument is payable if it is made in the name of that person." A.R.S. 
11   § 47-3405(B). Despite the employer's own liability, the employer may also recover from 
12   "the person paying the instrument or taking it for value or for collection [if the person] 
13   fails  to  exercise  ordinary  care  in  paying  or  taking  the  instrument  and  that  failure 
14   substantially contributes to loss resulting from the fraud." Id.

15                                                                        
    it  hired  Sotelo  as  an  employee  and  entrusted  him  with  responsibility  regarding  the 
16                                                                        
    invoices and the checks made payable to vendors. It also alleged that on some of those 
17                                                                        
    checks, Sotelo made fraudulent indorsements by writing the name of the vendor, and, on 
18                                                                        
    the rest, he simply fraudulently indorsed them by depositing the checks into his personal 
19                                                                        
    accounts.                                                            
20

26

Id.
